chapter.title: Classes
chapter.para: This chapter describes the public classes of python.cls: Python, whose instance is the environment object &py;, PyObject, the class of every Python object in Rexx, PyArrayProxy and PyKwArgs. The stream classes, PyOutputStream and PyInputStream, are described in . python.cls also requires boolean.cls, whose Boolean class is Python's bool in Rexx ().

section.title: Python Class
section.para: The Python class is a subclass of PyObject whose single instance, made when python.cls is loaded, is the environment object &py;. It is Python's builtins module: every message that is not one of the methods below is Python's builtin of that name, unchanged. .py~len(x) is len(x), .py~sorted(x) is sorted(x), and .py~IndexError is the exception class.

section.title: Builtins
section.para: Any other message is Python's builtin of that name, as for any PyObject (see ): a function is called, with the arguments if any; a class or an exception class is returned. .py~list is the class list; .py~list(x) calls it. To build a list, a tuple or a set from items, pass a Rexx Array: .py~list((1, 2)), .py~tuple(("a", 1)).
Python's builtins str, int and float are the methods below, which keep the result as a PyObject.

section.title: addCommandEnvironment
section.para: Makes the Python callable handler the ADDRESS environment name of this interpreter instance, from Rexx: the same as the Python side's , and the handler works the same way (). Registering a name again replaces its handler. A handler that is not callable, &nil; included, is an error (SYNTAX 98.900, a TypeError). See also .

example.title: Python class — addCommandEnvironment method
example.programlisting:
.py~addCommandEnvironment("len", .py~eval("lambda command, ctx: len(command)")) address len "abcd" say rc .py~removeCommandEnvironment("len") trace off -- no trace line for the failing command signal on failure address len "abcd" exit failure: say condition("C") rc
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: box
section.para: Returns a Python object of the given type, made from the text of value, never through the number rule (), and kept as a PyObject, so that passing it on keeps its type. The argument order is BSF4ooRexx's box. type is one of:

listitem.para: Python's int, float or complex of the text.
True for 1, False for 0; any other value is an error.
the bytes of the Rexx string.
decimal.Decimal or fractions.Fraction of the text.
a Python class or function, called with the text as a str.

section.para: The type names are case-insensitive. See also and .

example.title: Python class — box method
example.programlisting:
kind = .py~eval("lambda x: type(x).__name__") say kind~new(.py~box("str", 42)) kind~new(.py~box("float", 2)) say .py~box("bytes", "ab") .py~box("bool", 1) .py~box("complex", "1+2j") say .py~box("decimal", "0.1") + .py~box("decimal", "0.2") say .py~box(.py~import("pathlib")~PurePosixPath, "/tmp")~name
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: decimal
section.para: Returns decimal.Decimal(value), kept as a PyObject. A Rexx number goes as its text, so every digit is kept: Rexx numbers can have more digits than a Python float.

section.title: eval
section.para: Returns the value of the Python expression, evaluated with Python's eval in the namespace of the module __main__ (see ). The value follows .

section.title: exec
section.para: Runs the Python code, one statement or many (lines separated by line feeds), with Python's exec in the namespace of the module __main__. Returns &nil;. What the code defines stays in __main__, for later evals and execs and through .py~main.

example.title: Python class — eval, exec and main methods
example.programlisting:
.py~exec("def area(r): return 3 * r * r" || "0a"x || "unit = 'cm2'") say .py~eval("area(2)") .py~main~unit area = .py~main~getattr("area") -- the function, as a value say area~new(3)
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: extend
section.para: Makes the Rexx class, a subclass of PyObject, extend the Python class base, and returns the Python class it makes for it. The same as the routine ; see .

section.title: float
section.para: Returns Python's float(value), kept as a PyObject.

When value is a Rexx number that a double cannot hold, the result is an error, not an infinity or a zero: an OverflowError when it is too big (1E+999), a ValueError when it is not zero but would become zero (1E-999); in Rexx, SYNTAX 98.900. Infinity and NaN asked for by name, +infinity, -infinity, nan, still work, and excess digits are still rounded. The same holds for .py~box("float", value) and .py~box("complex", value).

section.title: import
section.para: Imports the Python module name and returns it, as a PyObject. A dotted name returns the submodule: .py~import("matplotlib.pyplot") is import matplotlib.pyplot, the module pyplot. A module is imported once per process, as in Python: later imports return the same module.

type says how Rexx strings go to the module: "number", the default, follows the number rule; "string" sends every Rexx string as a str in the calls made through the module and through everything reached from it. See .
See also .

example.title: Python class — import method
example.programlisting:
math = .py~import("math") say math~factorial(25) -- Python's int: no digits lost say .py~import("os.path")~getattr("__name__") \== "" json = .py~import("json") say json~dumps(.py~list((1, "two", .nil)))
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: int
section.para: Returns Python's int(value [, base]), kept as a PyObject.

section.title: kw
section.para: Returns a , the marker for keyword arguments, to be passed as the last argument of a call to Python. It is made from names and values in pairs, or from a collection: a Directory, a StringTable or any other MapCollection, whose indexes are the names. The names go to Python as written, in their case. See and .

section.title: main
section.para: Returns the module __main__, where eval and exec run. When a Python program runs the Rexx code, it is that program's main module.

section.title: raise
section.para: Raises a Python exception from Rexx code: exception is an exception object, or an exception class, which is called with the remaining arguments: .py~raise(.py~IndexError, i). In Rexx it is the condition SYNTAX 98.900, as when Python raises it, and Rexx code can trap it as any SYNTAX condition; if it goes back to Python, Python gets the exception itself. See .

section.title: redirectTo
section.para: Sends Rexx's standard streams to Python's. The same as the routine , with the same arguments; see .

section.title: removeCommandEnvironment
section.para: Makes the ADDRESS environment name, written in Python, unknown again: a command sent to it is then FAILURE with RC 30, as for an environment ooRexx does not know. A name that is not an environment written in Python is an error (SYNTAX 93.900). Returns nothing. The same as the Python side's ; see the example of .

section.title: str
section.para: Returns Python's str(value), kept as a PyObject, so that text that looks like a number goes to Python as text: d[.py~str("1")] is d["1"], where d["1"] would be d[1].

section.title: PyObject Class
section.para: A PyObject is a Python object, by reference: the proxy holds the Python object, and keeps it alive while Rexx holds the proxy. Rexx programs do not make them with new: the bridge makes one for every Python object that comes to Rexx and is not a simple value (). A Python object that comes to Rexx several times may come as different proxies; they compare ==, because == is Python's is.
Subclasses of PyObject are Rexx classes that extend Python classes; see .
All its methods are unguarded: a proxy has no Rexx state that changes, and Python's state is protected by Python's own lock.

row.entry: Methods inherited from Rexx's Object class (but see )

section.title: pyClass (Class Method)
section.para: Sent to a subclass of PyObject that extends a Python class, returns the Python class that made for it (or for its nearest superclass that has one); &nil; if there is none. Python code that makes the objects itself needs it: json~dumps(x, .py~kw("cls", .MyEncoder~pyClass)).

section.title: Arithmetic Methods
Comparison Methods
section.para: =, \=, <>, ><, <, >, <= and >= are Python's ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=. == and \== are Python's is and is not: the same Python object, however it came to Rexx. Comparing numpy arrays gives an array of bools, a boolean mask: a[a > 2].

section.title: Logical Methods
section.para: &, | and && are Python's &, | and ^: for sets, intersection, union and symmetric difference; for numpy's boolean arrays, element by element.

Returns Python's o[index]. Several indexes are a tuple: m[0, 1] is m[(0, 1)]. Positions count from 0, and negative positions from the end, as in Python. Indexes follow the number rule even when the object comes from a module imported as "string". See .
Python's o[index] = value.

section.title: copy, send, start, run, request
section.para: These are methods of Rexx's Object class that Python objects commonly have too: dict.copy, a generator's send, threading.Thread's start and run, the request of a socketserver handler. When the Python object has an attribute of that name, the message is Python's, as any other attribute; otherwise it is Rexx's. request is Python's only when it has no arguments, since Rexx's needs one.

example.title: PyObject class — copy is Python's when the object has it
example.programlisting:
d = .py~dict~new(.py~kw("a", 1)) e = d~copy -- dict.copy e["b"] = 2 say d e
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: getattr
section.para: Returns the attribute name, with its exact name, as Python's getattr(o, name): the attribute itself, never called. Use it when two names differ only in case (logging~getattr("INFO")), for names Rexx cannot write as symbols (o~getattr("__class__")), and to take a function or a method as a value.

section.title: hashCode
section.para: Returns a hash code consistent with ==, Python's identity, so that a PyObject can be the index of a Rexx Table, Set or Bag: two proxies of the same Python object find the same item.

section.title: invoke
section.para: Calls the attribute name, with its exact name, with the arguments (a PyKwArgs last for keyword arguments), and returns the result. With &nil; as the name, calls the object itself, as .

section.title: makeArray
section.para: Returns a Rexx Array of the items that iterating the object gives (Python's list(o), as a Rexx Array): a list's or a tuple's items, a dict's keys, a file's lines. It is what do x over o uses. The Array is a copy.

example.title: PyObject class — makeArray method
example.programlisting:
d = .py~dict~new(.py~kw("x", 1, "y", 2)) a = d~makeArray say a~items a[1] a[2] do k over d say k d[k] end
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: makeArrayProxy
section.para: Returns a for the object, a sequence (a list, a tuple, a one-dimensional numpy array): the sequence seen as a Rexx Array, counting from 1, that reads and writes through to the Python object.

section.title: new
section.para: Calls the object itself, Python's o(args), when it has no attribute new: a class makes an instance, a function is called. This is an instance method of each PyObject, not the class method of PyObject.

example.title: PyObject class — new method
example.programlisting:
fractions = .py~import("fractions") half = fractions~Fraction~new(1, 2) -- an instance say half half + fractions~Fraction~new(1, 3) square = .py~eval("lambda x: x * x") say square~new(12) -- a function, called
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: setattr
section.para: Sets the attribute name, with its exact name, as Python's setattr(o, name, value). Unlike o~name = value, it can create an attribute: Rexx cannot tell the case of a new name.

section.title: string
section.para: Returns Python's str(o), as a Rexx string: what say o shows.

section.title: unknown
section.para: Every other message is the Python attribute of that name, looked up without regard to case ():

listitem.para: o~name(args) calls it with the arguments;
o~name = value sets it; the attribute must exist ( creates one).

section.para: A name that matches no attribute is a Python AttributeError, raised as SYNTAX 98.900.

section.title: PyArrayProxy Class
section.para: A PyArrayProxy is a Python sequence (a list, a tuple, a one-dimensional numpy array) seen as a Rexx Array, counting from 1, as BSF4ooRexx's BSF_Array_Reference is for a Java array. It holds the Python object and reads and writes through it: nothing is copied. Positions go from 1 to items; outside them, [] and at return &nil;, as a Rexx Array's do, and []= and put at items + 1 append. Writing needs a sequence that can change: a list, not a tuple.
It is made with o~makeArrayProxy, or .PyArrayProxy~new(o).

row.entry: Methods inherited from Rexx's Object class

example.title: A Python list as a Rexx Array
example.programlisting:
l = .py~list((10, 20, 30)) a = l~makeArrayProxy say a[1] a~items a[4] -- from 1; outside: .nil a[2] = 21 -- writes through to the list a~append(40) say l do x over a; say x; end say a~remove(1) l
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: new (Class Method)
section.para: Returns a PyArrayProxy for pyobject, a PyObject that is a sequence. The same as pyobject~makeArrayProxy.
Replaces the item at position, from 1, or appends it when the position is items + 1. Any other position is an error.

section.title: allIndexes
section.para: Returns a Rexx Array of the positions, 1 to items.

section.title: allItems
section.para: Returns a Rexx Array of the items, a copy. The same as makeArray.

section.title: append
section.para: Appends item to the sequence, and returns its position, the new number of items.

section.title: at
section.para: The same as .

section.title: delete
section.para: The same as .

section.title: dimension
section.para: Without an argument, returns 1: the proxy has one dimension. With n, returns the size of dimension n: items for 1, 0 for any other.

section.title: first
section.para: Returns 1, the first position, or &nil; if the sequence is empty.

section.title: firstItem
section.para: Returns the first item, or &nil; if the sequence is empty.

section.title: hasIndex
section.para: Returns &true; if position is a whole number from 1 to items, &false; otherwise.

section.title: isEmpty
section.para: Returns &true; if the sequence has no items, &false; otherwise.

section.title: items
section.para: Returns the number of items, Python's len(o).

section.title: last
section.para: Returns the last position, items, or &nil; if the sequence is empty.

section.title: lastItem
section.para: Returns the last item, or &nil; if the sequence is empty.

section.title: makeArray
section.para: Returns a Rexx Array of the items, a copy. do x over a uses it.

section.title: put
section.para: The same as .

section.title: pyObject
section.para: Returns the Python sequence, the PyObject the proxy reads and writes.

section.title: remove
section.para: Removes the item at position and returns it; the items after it move one position down. Returns &nil; if there is no such position.

section.title: size
section.para: The same as .

section.title: string
section.para: Returns a PyArrayProxy followed by the Python sequence's string value.

section.title: supplier
section.para: Returns a Supplier of the items, with their positions as indexes (a snapshot).

section.title: PyKwArgs Class
section.para: A PyKwArgs holds keyword arguments: names and values, in order. As the last argument of a call to Python it is the keyword arguments of the call (); and make them. When Python calls a method of a Rexx class that extends a Python class with keyword arguments, the method gets them as a PyKwArgs, its last argument ().

section.title: new (Class Method)
section.para: Takes one argument, a Rexx Array with the arguments of : names and values in pairs, a MapCollection, or a Python dict. Programs use .py~kw(...) instead.
Returns the value of the argument name: the one with that exact name, else one with that name in any case, else &nil;.

section.title: items
section.para: Returns the number of keyword arguments.

section.title: names
section.para: Returns a Rexx Array of the names, in order.

section.title: values
section.para: Returns a Rexx Array of the values, in the order of the names.
